newsitem.title: GERMANY: Jobless surge causes alarm in Germany.
newsitem.headline: Jobless surge causes alarm in Germany.

text.p: A surge in German unemployment ignited a heated debate on Friday as newspaper editorials criticised Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government for lacking the vision to solve the problem.
Calls grew louder for fast and effective action as dailies devoted much of their front pages to news that unemployment leaped by half a million in January to a post-war record of 4.66 million.

"The unemployment numbers are catastrophic and it is clear the Kohl government is no longer able to solve our problems," said Gerhard Schroeder, state premier in Lower Saxony and a leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD)."Kohl has become part of the problem."
The Federal Labour Office said on Thursday that unemployment climbed to 12.2 percent in January from 10.8 percent in December, the highest in 64 years.

Kohl tried as usual to put an optimistic spin on the news, saying the unemployment rate would soon begin to fall. But he admitted the figures were the bleakest he had seen in his 14 years as chancellor.
Kohl, who is often ridiculed for forecasting unemployment would be halved by 2000, retreated on Friday by saying that this was only a goal and not a forecast.

"This is a goal and we have no reason to abandon this goal," Kohl told a news conference on Friday. He said he planned to use this year when there were no distractions of elections to concentrate on tax and pension reform measures.

"In the coming weeks we want to push forward the tax reforms and seek out discussions with the opposition Social Democrats," Kohl said. "I am certain that once we have a decision on tax reform the atmosphere for investment will improve enormously."
Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl tried to fend off attacks on the government's policies.

"It is wrong to say we have misjudged the situation," he told ZDF television. "The January figures are unacceptable. But the measures we introduced should mean that improvements can be expected in the second half of the year."
Conservative and liberal newspapers filled their columns with warnings that major steps were needed to resolve the unemployment crisis.

They belittled the fact that government and opposition agree on only one idea -- cutting overtime hours -- to reduce unemployment, and blasted political leaders for failing to understand that old prescriptions no longer work.

"Anyone who takes a sober look at unemployment should realise that it will be much harder to resolve than previously thought," Die Welt wrote. "The core of the problem is that labour in Germany is too inflexible and too expensive."

The conservative Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) said comparisons with the high unemployment of the ill-fated Weimar Republic, which preceded Adolf Hitler's Third Reich, were out of place. But it said lower taxes, deregulation, a smaller government and new thinking were needed.

"There are no longer any patent recipes," the FAZ said. "But what will definitely fail is the muddled attempt to push the social security system of yesterday into the business world of tomorrow. That will lead to a huge accident whose result will be mass unemployment."
The liberal Sueddeutsche Zeitung called Kohl's promise to halve unemployment a "4.66-million-man lie".
"Everyone is blaming everyone and everything else -- high labour costs, too much overtime, unpatriotic companies moving jobs abroad and the government with its misguided policies," the paper wrote.
